transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-03
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Ellis (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (BlueNorth - Head of Platform), Priya Rao (BlueNorth - SRE Lead), Ben Torres (BlueNorth - CTO)

Summary:
Quick, pragmatic console walkthrough focusing on request tracing, error analysis, and request-log stitching for an intermittent production failure affecting their routing microservice. Goal was to show Redwood Console features for correlating traces, KV cache and prefix cache behavior, and propose pilot steps.

Topics covered:
- How Redwood Console captures and surfaces request journeys, including request-id stitching and span maps
- Error analysis: stack traces vs model output anomalies vs infra timeouts
- Request log enrichment: attaching prompt/eval metadata, partial token payload visibility, and privacy knobs
- Debugging flows: replays, request playback, and causal trace filtering
- Pilot scoping: sample export format, SLAs, and compliance (SOC 2, KMS)

Action items (as discussed verbally):
- Jordan: export of the failing request samples + trace IDs from last 7 days; include suspected input variations (due 2026-05-06)
- Samira: run traces through Redwood Console sandbox, produce a 2-page findings note and config suggestions (due 2026-05-10)
- Marcus/Priya: provision a small VPC peering test env and share network contacts for pilot (target week of 2026-05-18)

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, quick intros, I'll let Samira do a little context then we can jump into your failure pattern.
[00:12] Samira: Hi all, Samira from Redwood infra, I focus on observability and the Console. Marcus, I got the note you sent — intermittent 504s in the routing service?
[00:20] Marcus: Yeah, exactly. We'll get a spike every morning around 03:00 UTC and, uh, some requests blow up with timeout. It's weird because the CPU on the pods doesn't move much.
[00:31] Priya: And just to call out, we see token cost anomalies — some requests go way higher token count even though input is small. So maybe cache or prefix replay is behaving weird.
[00:42] Samira: Got it. So today we'll show how Console stitches request logs, how you can open a request journey and see KV cache hits/misses, and then how to run a replay. Quick callouts: term mismatch in transcripts — KV cache sometimes gets transcribed as K-V cash in our export so, forgive the bad audio.
[00:58] Ben: (laughs) heard it before.
[01:03] Jordan: Cool. Marcus, can you briefly run through your stack and where Redwood would sit?
[01:09] Marcus: Sure. We have a fleet of routing microservices in GKE, they call out to an inference service — right now that's an in-house endpoint running a quantized model on our GPUs. Some traffic is still going via OpenAI for exploratory features. We're evaluating Redwood to unify serving and get better latency/cost predictability and tracing.
[01:30] Jordan: Helpful. What's the success criteria for you here? Lower P95 latency, consistent token cost, and ability to debug these intermittent 504s with request-forensics?
[01:39] Priya: Exactly. Also — strong audit trails for compliance, SSO integration (SAML), and KMS for key management.
[01:46] Samira: Good — Console has audit logs, full request-level trace retention on Dedicated, and integrations for customer-managed KMS when you're on Private or Dedicated.
[01:55] Marcus: Two quick asks: can the Console show prompt redaction in traces, and can we replay just the failing portion without re-executing external side effects?
[02:06] Samira: Yes on both. We have prompt redaction controls and a replay sandbox that replays token generation locally avoiding external HTTP calls — it's labeled "dry-run" in the UI.
[02:17] Priya: Show us that?
[02:19] Samira: Sure — I'll share my screen. (screen share) Ok, here's the request timeline. You'll see the top-level request node, then child spans for prefix-cache lookup, tokenization, model call, and postprocessing.
[02:35] Samira: Note this particular trace shows a long tail in the model call span — down to ms resolution. You can click the span and get per-step logs, and see an event that says "kv_cache_miss" — sometimes transcribed as K-V miss in older exports.
[02:49] Marcus: That kv_cache_miss is interesting — in our infra we saw a mismatch in key encoding after a deployment. Could be a serialization problem. Can Console surface the exact cache key that missed?
[02:59] Samira: We can surface a hashed key by default, and with permission we can show the normalized key form. We generally default to hashing to avoid exposing PII. There's a toggle in request settings.
[03:12] Ben: How about token counts showing up higher?
[03:15] Samira: There are two places: prefix/kv caching can cause duplicate prompt segments if the cache TTL is short or if you have overlapping prefixes. The Console shows token burn per-span so you can see which span consumed extra tokens.
[03:30] Priya: Can you drill into an example request?
[03:33] Samira: Yeah. I'm opening one of your exported traces. (pause) Ok, here's id 7f1a2... I see a retry loop in the client that fired a second model call after a soft 429 — that explains the extra tokens. The first call had a transient 429 from their proxy and the client retried synchronously.
[03:49] Marcus: That rings true — our retry backoff was not honoring 429 Retry-After.
[03:54] Jordan: That's a great find — so it's not a model runtime issue, it's client-side retry semantics amplifying token cost.
[04:01] Samira: Right. But also notice a pattern where some requests show a large serialization latency before the model call — likely due to blocking I/O in the microservice.
[04:12] Priya: About the production 504s though, do we see a correlation?
[04:15] Samira: I can run a query across traces for request paths that had both a model span timeout and downstream HTTP timeouts. The Console correlation panel will show co-occurring errors.
[04:26] Ben: And metrics? Can we pivot from a trace to the per-route SLO dashboard?
[04:30] Samira: Yes, top-right there's a "Jump to SLO" that filters the route-level dashboard by the same tags. You can then open the flamegraph and see where percentiles are shifting.
[04:41] Marcus: Let's say we want to run a replay on the failing requests but with model quantization variants, like q4 and int8. Can the replay target different model variants?
[04:52] Samira: For sure — replay supports model variants in the sandbox. It will re-run the token generation path with a specified model binary. Keep in mind tokenization differences can slightly alter outputs; we show a diff view.
[05:04] Priya: Any caveats when replaying? Side effects?
[05:07] Samira: The replay has a "no-side-effects" mode. For external webhooks we stub the calls. For database writes, we can mirror the payload to a mock or skip altogether.
[05:16] Marcus: Ok good. One of our security folks will ask about logs retention and encryption.
[05:20] Jordan: We have per-account retention controls. On Dedicated or Private you can meet their retention and bring-your-own KMS. For hosted we encrypt at rest and in transit, SOC 2 Type II, and we can provide more audit artifacts under NDA.
[05:34] Ben: How granular is RBAC? We need to restrict playback and unredacted prompt views to a small group.
[05:40] Samira: RBAC is role-based at route and team level. Playback and view-unredacted are separate privileges. You can bind through SAML groups or manually in Console.
[05:50] Priya: Let's try a live search across traces for error code 504 and the route /v1/routing/*
[05:56] Samira: Typing... ok filtering now. I'm seeing 18 traces in the window for the last 7 days. If we add a correlation for model_span_error > 0 we get five overlapping traces where both a model_span_error and downstream 504 occurred.
[06:13] Marcus: Show one of them.
[06:16] Samira: Opening trace 2026-04-28-09:17. The visualization shows two parallel spans — model call and downstream HTTP. The downstream span has a 504 and the model span ended a bit after due to backpressure on the client.
[06:33] Jordan: That backpressure explains the 504s — the client waited for model response and the upstream gateway timed out. Do you have a gateway timeout of 30s?
[06:41] Marcus: Yeah, edge timeout is 25s. The model p95 is normally 200ms but under load we saw spikes to 26s in one incident.
[06:49] Samira: That spike is suspicious — could be an outlier host or GPU contention. Console will surface host-level metrics pinned to the trace so you can see GPU util, mem, and any migration events.
[07:00] Priya: Could quantization or kernel selection cause a spike like that?
[07:04] Samira: Possibly. If the runtime flips to a slower kernel path say for long context lengths or missing fused kernels, latency can jump. Also if KV cache is being evicted aggressively you may see repeated warmups.
[07:18] Ben: You mentioned automatic fallback policies earlier. Can we set a rule to route to a cheaper model if p95 exceeds a threshold?
[07:25] Samira: Yes. We have smart routing polices: route by latency or cost. You can automatic-fallback to a smaller model or to a hosted variant in another region. We also support a warm standby pool.
[07:36] Marcus: On the pilot — we want to start with a small percentage of traffic and validate observability. What data do you need from us?
[07:42] Jordan: The main things: sample traces of failing requests (request ids), a small ACL'd S3 export so we can ingest traces into the sandbox, and a rough QPS during the 03:00 UTC window.
[07:54] Marcus: I'll get that out.
[07:56] Priya: One more question: can Console produce a CSV of correlation results so we can drop into our incident tracker?
[08:01] Samira: Yes exportable CSV/JSON. Also we have an API endpoint if you want programmatic pulls.
[08:08] Ben: Any known issues integrating with GKE ingress health checks?
[08:12] Samira: Not specific ones; most customers use the Redis-backed prefix cache we offer or their own K-V store. If your ingress strips headers we can recommend a header-preservation policy.
[08:25] Marcus: Are there rate limits on replay? We might want to replay a few thousand requests in a spike test.
[08:31] Samira: In the hosted sandbox we throttle heavy replays; on Dedicated you can provision a replay job with a defined capacity. We'll size it in pilot.
[08:42] Jordan: Quick detour — Priya you mentioned client retries causing double token burns. Would it help to instrument the client to set a 429 backoff?
[08:52] Priya: Yes we'll do that. We'll also add more granular logs to include request-id in the routing service.
[08:59] Samira: Perfect — that will make correlation trivial. Also when you export traces, include both the raw payload and any enriched metadata you can (headers masked if needed).
[09:10] Marcus: Ok, let's talk compliance: we need SOC 2 docs and a security questionnaire — how fast can you turn those around?
[09:15] Jordan: We can share SOC 2 and our security pack within 48 hours; for a security questionnaire we typically go through our security team and often do a live review.
[09:24] Ben: If we go Dedicated or Private, what are typical lead times?
[09:28] Jordan: Dedicated spin-up is 4-6 weeks with expedited options; Private on-prem is longer, depends on infra. We can work with your procurement.
[09:38] Priya: For the pilot can Redwood recommend configuration for batching and cache TTL to keep p95 < 500ms?
[09:44] Samira: Yes, we'll include concrete config suggestions in the findings doc — batch max size, max latency window, cache TTL, quantization profile for your model shape.
[09:55] Marcus: One last thing: can we get a trace export that includes the exact token-level diff so we can reproduce the cost spike locally?
[10:02] Samira: We include token-level diffs in the replay artifacts. We can also provide a token burn per-span CSV.
[10:11] Jordan: Great. let's go to wrap-up — quick recap and next steps.
[10:16] Jordan: Recap: Samira found client retries and a serialization latency contributing to token spikes; Console correlates model and downstream errors and supports redaction, replays, and model-variant testing in the sandbox. Action items: Jordan will collect the trace exports, Samira will run sandbox analysis, BlueNorth will provision a minimal peering for pilot.
[10:34] Marcus: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[10:36] Ben: Thanks.
[10:37] Priya: Thanks.
[10:38] Jordan: We'll follow up with the export template and a calendar invite for the pilot scoping. Bye.

End of transcript.
